member of the commission. madam president, mr rapporteur, ladies and gentlemen, allow me to begin by thanking the rapporteur, mr zarzalejos, for the work he has done in recent months on this report on the european arrest warrant. i am delighted to have the opportunity to be here with you today to discuss this instrument which is essential for the area of freedom, security and justice. the european arrest warrant is the most effective criminal justice instrument in europe. it is an essential tool for transferring persons suspected of having committed an offence from one member state of the union to another. it ensures that suspects and convicted persons cannot escape justice within the union. as evidenced by the number of warrants issued and executed and the considerable increase in the number of questions referred to the court of justice in this area, the european arrest warrant is widely used by legal practitioners and the court's case law has made a significant contribution to strengthening the uniform application of this instrument and to ensuring respect for fundamental rights. of course, as the commission already pointed out in its july 2020 report, there is room for further improvement in the functioning of the arrest warrant. this is also recognised by the member states, which adopted conclusions on this in december 2020. in your report you also included a number of suggestions. i would like to stress at this stage that the commission has taken note of this report with great interest, particularly in the context of our work on improving the arrest warrant. let me give you some concrete examples. first, on respect for fundamental rights, i want to stress that there is no doubt that european arrest warrants need to respect our fundamental values. the system is structured on that basis. as you know, the respect of fundamental rights is underlined in the framework decision itself. clear standards for its application have also been set by the case law of the court of justice. in particular, the court has confirmed that a refusal is possible on fundamental rights grounds as regards detention conditions and the right to a fair trial, as well as in exceptional cases. furthermore, respect for fundamental rights is also enshrined in the eu's procedural-wide directives, which have to be fully transposed and implemented in all member states. but our work is not limited to that. the commission intends to continue its reflection on possible additional guarantees for the protection of fundamental rights. as your report has highlighted, the issues of admissibility of evidence and pre-trial detention are particularly relevant and require a thorough analysis. we will carry out studies on these topics to examine more closely the existing problems and the need for possible european rules. let me turn to your reports proposal: the modification of the list of offences for which no double criminality check is required. firstly, i would point out that the list as it stands covers most of the offences that member states consider serious offences within the eu. having said that, the commission will look into this issue through a gap analysis to see whether further offences would need to be added or whether a more precise definition of the offences as mentioned in the current list is needed. as you know, the commission is also working on an initiative to expand the list of eurocrimes with regard to hate speech and violence against women. this will result in more common eu offences no longer requiring a double criminality check. moreover, any possible modification of this list would not only affect the functioning of the european arrest warrant, but would likely also have an impact on all of the relevant material recognition instruments that contain a similar list, such as the european investigation order. another point. the commission welcomes the soft law measures recommended in your report. as you know, the commission is already providing funding for training and networks on the european arrest warrant, and we intend to continue to do so. we also share your focus on the importance of reliable data. the commission is currently investigating the possibilities to expand the digital actions platforms to judicial cooperation instruments such as the european arrest warrant. this will lead to better comparable data in the future. we agree with your focus on the importance of direct contacts and consultation between judicial authorities. i hope we can also improve the situation by a closer alignment with all relevant parties through the european arrest warrant coordination group that was recently set up by the commission. finally, we have started revising the handbook on the european arrest warrant. it will contain an update of the 33 new judgments delivered by the court of justice on the instruments since the last version of the handbook in 2017. before concluding, let me return to one last point which i consider to be fundamental. the commission attaches the utmost importance to the full and correct transposition of the framework decision on the european arrest warrant. so far, we have launched infringement procedures against seven member states on transposition issues and will continue, if necessary, this year. we welcome the fact that some member states are planning to amend their national legislation to address the identified shortcomings. this is essential work if we are to achieve the optimal functioning of the arrest warrant throughout the union. i thank you for your attention and i now look forward to hearing your questions and comments on this instrument which, i repeat, is probably the most important instrument in the functioning of our criminal justice throughout the european union and of course the cooperation of the member states in this area.
the committee on constitutional affairs has adopted a number of amendments to the draft law. madam president, commissioner, dear rapporteur, the european arrest warrant is one of the pillars of the schengen area; it is a pillar for security, but also for freedom and for the fundamental rights of all europeans. there is no free movement without cooperation and without trust in security and the fight against crime. but today, 18 years later, and speaking as a member of the committee on constitutional affairs, the mandate remains one of the best instruments for constitutional integration of our internal legal systems. but, having come of age, the european arrest warrant is ready for more. it must be brought into line with the treaty of lisbon. he needs to be adapted to the new world of crime. it needs more harmonization. as in the schengen area, so in the area of security, freedom and justice, the european arrest warrant needs a strategy for the future, a strategy that is up to date, in accordance with the treaty of lisbon.
the european parliament has been asked to take a decision on the future of the european union, and the european parliament has been asked to take a decision on the future of the union. the european arrest warrant is one such instrument. and it's proven to be a successful tool. whereas at the beginning of this century it took an average of one year to exchange a suspect within the eu, today it takes an average of one and a half months. justice is now eight times faster, thanks in part to the european arrest warrant, a little-known but very important part of our joint cooperation in the field of justice in the eu. it is true that the context has changed in the last 20 years. the digital transformation has also changed the nature of crime and there is therefore a need to adapt this instrument to the present times, for example by adding crimes already mentioned which have become more relevant in recent years, but also by looking closely at conditions of detention, proportionality and procedural safeguards, and an absolute prerequisite for cooperation in this area protection of the rule of law in all our member states. yes, there are challenges to the european arrest warrant and mr zarzalejos has spelled them out very well in his report, but it does not detract from the fact that - as the report also says - the european arrest warrant has been, is and will continue to be an extremely important instrument.
the adoption of the european arrest warrant by a governmental framework decision in 2002 was a giant step forward in the area of freedom, security and justice. it is a political decision by governments, which overcomes the old extradition procedure by means of a judicial procedure which is guaranteed, binding and directly operative, and which does not require a double-incrimination test in a list of thirty-two offences. since then it has been a success story: 43 000 european arrest warrants have been successfully completed, reducing extradition times from the old two years to an average of 40 to 50 days. however, the passage of time - the enlargement of the european union from 15 to 27 and 28 members in 2002 - has made it more complex, but also more unequal, and has shown, in the succession of crises since then, the erosion of the principles of mutual trust and mutual recognition on which the area of freedom, security and justice enshrined in the treaty of lisbon, article 82 of which binds all the member states, is based. that is exactly why the committee on civil liberties, justice and home affairs, which i chair, has adopted this own-initiative report: precisely to examine, re-evaluate and re-impulse the european arrest warrant, learning from the lessons of experience. this means addressing the need for training to implement the european detention manual, addressing the current divergences between the different procedural systems and their safeguards in the member states, harmonising european criminal law... but also extending the list, free from double criminality, to deal with crimes such as gender-based violence, environmental crimes or crimes against humanity or genocide and violence against the constitutional integrity of the member states. all this while respecting the principles of proportionality, necessity and minimum intervention, but above all by reviving the european order to overcome its restrictive refusal, which is prohibited by the case law of the court of justice of the european union, and by ensuring that in no case does the guarantee of fundamental rights obscure a review by the requested state of the quality of the judicial organisation or of the competence of the requested states in judicial matters. if this initiative is adopted - as we hope - in this european parliament, it will be up to the commission to take the legislative initiative. because that is what an own-initiative report is all about: to bind the commission to bring forward an update to a code of european judicial cooperation in criminal matters.
on behalf of the renew group. madam president, ladies and gentlemen, today is one of those days when we can feel the usefulness of this parliament. we started the legislature with a clear idea: the european arrest warrant needed to be revised to minimise, to improve, of course to avoid impunity in the schengen area, to better protect victims of crime in the european union and to also improve the safeguards for persons involved in crime. thanks to the loyal collaboration between the major political groups in this house, we have an implementation report which clearly shows us the blind spots of this cornerstone of judicial cooperation in the european union, the euro order. minimising - as i say - impunity in the schengen area is key. and it also means adapting judicial cooperation to the new times, to the digital revolution, to the threats, to the new threats to the rule of law. because the world is changing and our standards must improve with those changes, with those mutations also of crime. we therefore want a more proportionate mechanism, which means not using the instrument for minor crimes, but at the same time being effective in prosecuting the most serious crimes, such as threats to the public order of the member states and crimes against the constitutional integrity committed with the use of violence, not forgetting other crimes against humanity, genocide and war crimes. as legislators, we must continue to improve this mechanism and i am personally committed to working on it.
for the greens/efa group madam president, andrew symeou is a british citizen who was charged with involvement in the death of a man in greece and handed over to greek justice by a european arrest warrant in july 2009. he then spent ten months in appalling detention conditions and was prevented from returning home until july 2011, when he was exonerated. two years of a life wasted, away from loved ones and with a violent interruption of his studies. although this case is emblematic and a little better known than the others, it is not an isolated one. the consequences for people's lives are dramatic. it is difficult to have figures on these abuses, which are due to a variety of reasons: disproportionate use for minor offences, failure to respect fundamental rights or simple police error that a remote hearing could have demonstrated. however, the european arrest warrant is an indispensable tool for the development of this judicial cooperation which is the guarantee of a true european union, and it avoids many of the problems associated with traditional extradition. that is why we must evaluate it with the utmost seriousness and sincerity. the proper functioning of cooperation instruments is based on the principle of mutual recognition and implies mutual trust in the legal systems of the member states, but the deterioration of the rule of law and freedoms in our union no longer encourages blind trust. in some cases, judicial independence is weakened, as in hungary. it is even being questioned in poland. today, the immense responsibility lies with the judge concerned by the request alone to decide whether or not to extradite a person to a member state, where his rights may not be respected, without real european support or resources at his disposal to investigate and justify his refusal. the european parliament must therefore send a strong signal that the application of the mandate is accompanied by strong procedural guarantees, both in the issuing and the executing states. above all, we must guard against any political exploitation of these tools and, in this context, we deplore the occasional lack of retreat on the part of some members of the european parliament and the importance that spain's national interests have taken over from a global watchful eye. it is proposed to add the mention of the crime against the constitutional integrity of a country to the list of offences requiring neither verification nor debate. this opens up a terribly dangerous breach. such a provision would endanger many political activists in the european union, as the notion of constitutional integrity can lead to so many interpretations, our constitutions are so different. we cannot allow conflicts of interest in one member state to have a policing impact on the whole european process. the european arrest warrant can be a very effective and positive tool for victims, for a european union which guarantees rights and for confronting mafias, major crimes, violence and terrorism. but it must be used wisely, with vigilance and proportionality. national courts must be trained, alternative procedures used, fundamental rights respected, interpretation ensured in proceedings, and improved conditions of detention. we also thank the rapporteur for including our proposals on fundamental rights and we thank the commissioner for pointing out the necessary developments and the necessary conditions of justice.

in writing. – one of the best ways to ensure the prosperity and wellbeing of european citizens for generations to come is by completing the single market. the eu single market is one of our greatest strengths: it stimulates competition and trade, improves efficiency, raises quality and helps cut prices. it accounts for 450 million consumers and 22.5 million small and medium-sized enterprises (smes). however, we still have to take some steps before the true completion of the single market. an area in which the single market can be strengthened is in the free movement of services. services account for 70% of all economic activity in the eu and create 90% of new employment. cross-border trade in services, on the other hand, generates only 6.5% of the eu’s gdp. this shows a clear need to further stimulate the free movement of services by effectively and coherently implementing existing legislation, the use of public procurement where needed to reduce the costs of cross-border procurement for smes, micro-enterprises and self-employed, and the use of the european semester to remove administrative and regulatory barriers when presenting country-specific recommendations. completing and strengthening the single market is also crucial to a resilient economic recovery from the covid-19 crisis.

reporting for the committee on the environment, public health and consumer protection, mrs lulling, member of the commission. - mr president, i am very pleased to be able to present this report to you today on a subject which is very close to my heart. i am an environmentalist, the daughter and wife of a sailor, and a friend of many fishermen in my area. while some people here, including in this parliament, are still trying to oppose fishing and the protection of fisheries resources and biodiversity, the fishermen i meet have understood that they depend on it. this is the main idea of my report. more fish in the sea means both achieving our environmental goals and protecting biodiversity. but it also means that fishermen can continue to fish in the long term. the year 2020 was to be the year when the european union was to achieve good environmental status for its seas and the year when all fish stocks were to be exploited at sustainable levels. since the reform of the common fisheries policy in 2013, real progress has been made but the objectives set are not being achieved and there is urgency. the situation is very different in the atlantic and mediterranean areas. a while ago i met with fishermen in brittany and normandy. they explained that some species, such as the st. james's shell, were doing very well, but they were seeing other phenomena, such as the proliferation of sea spiders due to warming waters and climate change. the situation in the mediterranean is alarming. over 80% of fish stocks are still overfished. so we have to go further. the scientific knowledge of fish populations, but also of the interactions between different species, needs to be strengthened. the commission has also proposed that the fishing fleet should be able to use the catch quotas set out in the tacs for the stock of cod and haddock in the baltic sea. all quotas must also be set in a transparent manner and never beyond scientific recommendations and levels to achieve maximum sustainable yield. i also proposed in this report to study the relevance of new indicators such as the mer (maximum economic return). it aims to fish below the level of the msy (maximum sustainable yield). this would improve the resilience of fish stocks and the economic viability of fisheries in the medium and long term. in preparing this report, i met with many stakeholders from the fishing industry and environmental associations. i am lucky to live by the sea, close to several marine protected areas, including cap roux in the var. as a fisherman was showing me around the marine protected area, we saw a trawler coming in to fish right in the middle of the area. his observation, which i have heard repeated by many fishermen and associations i have met, is that many of the marine protected areas in europe are only protected on paper: no monitoring, incomplete management plans when they exist... using different methods, ngos and scientists have come to the same conclusion: while we boast of having protected 10% of europe's seas, less than 2% are actually protected. the biodiversity strategy sets the objective of having 30% of european waters covered by high-level marine protected areas. this is a great thing and is in line with the recommendations of the scientists, but it will only be a large-scale eco-bleaching operation if these protected areas do not have real management plans and control measures. the acceptance of marine protected areas by fishermen is a key element of their success. all actors must be involved in the establishment, management and monitoring of these marine protected areas, starting with fishermen and scientists. so it is also necessary to explain: 30% of marine protected areas, this does not mean that fishermen are excluded from 30% of the maritime spaces. within the 10% that will benefit from strong protections, there should be areas where all fishing and economic activity is prohibited, but in the majority of protected areas only the most destructive fishing techniques should be restricted according to local characteristics and the seasons. there are examples. very few fish restocking areas have been established since their creation in 2014. however, there are fish recovery areas, such as the one in jabuka/pomo set up in 2017 by the general fisheries commission for the mediterranean, which are already bearing fruit. the project is located in a strategic location where certain species, notably hake, breed, and has helped to restore populations of this species, visible beyond the marine protected area, and has won the support of local fishermen. let us take inspiration from this for all marine protected areas. fish populations are also faced with climate change and various sources of pollution, such as wastewater treatment, pesticide use in agriculture, cigarette butts thrown into the sea or from beaches, sunscreen, etc. we need to study these phenomena better so that we can act on them. it is also important that the resources of the future emff be mobilised towards the objectives i have mentioned: the establishment of these high-level marine protected areas, their management and control, research on selectivity, training of stakeholders, such as for example sworn guards. i invite the commission to use this report for the implementation of the biodiversity strategy, which must be translated into binding legal texts, for the action plan for the conservation of fisheries resources and the protection of marine ecosystems that you announced for this year and for the evaluation of the common fisheries policy, also in the coming months. i would like to conclude by thanking my various fictitious rapporteurs whose spirit of compromise has made it possible to have a complete report. i was pleased to work with you on this report, even though the negotiations were mainly conducted through our teams. thank you to the ngos, to the fishermen who helped me with this report. let us continue this work for nature, for fishermen and for more fish in the sea.
on behalf of the ppe group. mr president, commissioner, how can we not share the objective of preserving and restoring marine species as mrs roose's report calls for? a few weeks ago i was in mayotte and réunion, meeting fishermen who have been fishing in these tropical waters for generations, and i would like to express their concern here: we have never seen marine species so vulnerable. of the four species of tuna in the indian ocean, only one was in a state of alert only five years ago. today, only one is out of danger. stocks of all other species are collapsing, so there is an urgent need to react. the first priority is to find the way back to a sound, controlled and environmentally friendly fishing, as well as to the wisdom inherited from its own tradition. fishing is a wonderful relationship with the balance of life and not with a material that is available indefinitely. innovation and technology must enable us to extend and pass on this heritage. let's be clear, the drifting fish-gathering devices that have proliferated in recent years have had a major impact on the survival of species. they divert marine migration, trap young fish, increase bycatch and contribute to marine pollution. we must find a way back together to a shared responsibility with all the actors concerned. secondly, the european union must make its partners accept clear and respected common rules. we must put all our weight in the balance together to get out of the denial in which many third countries still persist, which can only lead to disaster. we can only achieve this with real firmness by demanding regular checks like those which are currently being carried out on european fisheries. finally, we need to improve our knowledge of these species by investing ever more in science, with the support of fishermen. we are not here to believe that fishing is a form of crime against the sea, and it is only with fishermen, the first explorers of the oceans, that we can learn more about them and preserve species and biodiversity better.

president-in-office of the council. – madam president, honourable members, commissioner, i would like to thank the european parliament for keeping on the agenda the difficult situation at our borders and the humanitarian situation of refugees and migrants and giving visibility to this matter. with the impact of the pandemic situation this matter demands even more our committed attention to ensure that we live up to our values, that people arriving at the external borders of the union are treated with respect and dignity. since the start of our presidency a few days ago, we have had the possibility already amongst member states to address one humanitarian emergency situation, the one in the lipa camp in bosnia—herzegovina, but we know quite well that more needs to be done. our presidency is closely monitoring the situation on all migratory routes and we will continue to do so throughout the semester. in 2020 the total number of illegal border crossings at the eu external borders was estimated as 97 000, at the lowest level in seven years. however, while the eastern mediterranean route saw a very significant decrease of nearly 80%, arrivals on the central mediterranean route increased 145%, and overall arrivals in spain also increased 29% compared to 2019. i would like to touch upon developments in greece, in bosnia-herzegovina, in libya and in the canary islands. in january and february last year high numbers of migrants arrived in greece, creating very difficult conditions of overcrowding the islands, in particular the island of lesbos. the number of migrants present on the islands reached a peak of more than 40 000 people. the greek authorities undertook many efforts to strengthen the border controls after the unrest, equal efforts were also made to improve the reception conditions which suffered from the overcrowding of the camps. the arrival of the covid-19 crisis and the fire in the moria camp in september only exacerbated the situation, calling for immediate action. some improvements have been made. the number of migrants in the centre of the island is now approximately 15 000 people. eu funding is in place. more permanent reception structures are in the pipeline and a joint task force has been established to ensure adequate living conditions and faster procedures. the situation remains volatile in this region of the world. the political climate between the eu and our neighbour turkey plays a significant role in the stability of the region and hence on the arrival of migrants, and we need to continue monitoring the situation quite closely. during the next six months, we will continue to devote also much attention to the migratory situation in the western balkans region, in particular in bosnia-herzegovina where around 5 800 migrants and refugees are currently present, mainly in the north west. following strong advocacy by a number of actors, including the eu and humanitarian agencies, we note that the local authorities are making considerable efforts to address the situation, and have now identified an interim solution for some 900 individuals in dire conditions at the lipa site. however, no long-term solution has been identified. we will need to continue to support the authorities but also urge them to provide better reception conditions and efficient services, including access to the asylum procedures for people in need of international protection. regarding the central mediterranean route, conditions for migrants in libya continue to be dire. to alleviate the suffering of migrants and refugees in urban settings or in detention centres in libya, the eu and individual member states have funded projects via the eu trust fund for africa, our implementing partners unhcr and iom continue to do a very important work. this includes also the iom programme for voluntary returns of countries of origin, which has resumed after a long break due to the covid crisis. the same applies for the work of the unhcr to evacuate detained persons of concern to either niger or rwanda, with a view to resettlement in the eu or other receiving countries. let me also mention the situation in the canary islands, where thousands of irregular migrants arrived in october and november in huge numbers, overwhelming for a period the capacity of the authorities to register, identify and accommodate them. the migrants, half of whom are moroccan and half of whom are sub-saharan, come from sub-saharan countries, arrived in small boats and were rescued at sea. the influx led to the deployment of the frontex officers to assist in the first registration and in the notification procedures. a contract was signed with easo to also assist in improving reception capacities, and we strongly encourage the operational and technical support by eu agencies in front line member states. i would like to stress that the humanitarian situation at our external borders is a cause of great concern that needs our attention and more needs to be done, and i trust the commissioner would also elaborate on the comprehensive assistance that the eu is providing at our external borders to improve the situation. but before i finish, honourable members, i would like to say that the presidency is committed to finding better solutions as regards migration and refugee flows. we will give priority to the new pact and migration and asylum and the initiatives that it contains, aiming to establish a common migration management mechanism that is effective, resilient and reliable and safeguards human rights, based on a fair sharing of efforts and obligations. and we are committed to achieving results on the basis of the commission’s last package of proposals. and i say we will foster the deepening of the partnerships between the eu and the countries of origin and transit, including through constructive dialogue and the development of a policy to promote legal migration channels. this is a sustainable alternative and takes into account the objective of integrating migrants, especially unaccompanied minors. we will also aim to implement the valletta declaration and its action plan together with the accompanying regional dialogue and to follow up on the global compacts for migration and refugees, and in this context we intend to organise in lisbon a ministerial conference on migration flows. member of the commission. – mr president, i would like to thank the committee on employment and social affairs, and particularly the rapporteur, for the work on this legislative own-initiative report on a very important and sensitive issue: the right to disconnect. indeed, the report addresses this important issue, which is related to the profound changes in the world of work – profound changes dominated by the digitalisation of many jobs and by the way people work and are connected. in the last few years we have witnessed a sustained growth in telework and an accelerated adoption of icts for work purposes. with the lockdowns due to the covid-19 crisis, this gained much more prominence, and it will likely remain a permanent feature in the work organisation. digitalisation has created, indeed, new businesses, new opportunities, new ways of working, living and consuming. it has led to productivity increases, to more flexibility for workers and businesses, and in the context of the pandemic, allowed many workers and many companies just to continue their activities. so if there is, on one hand, an important advance by the digitalisation of the european economy, we have also to have a very, very keen look at the upholding of working conditions and labour law. the new economy cannot develop outside the normal framework of labour law, including also working time. this is not just a social dimension; it’s also an economic one, so we have really to maintain a balance between the development of digitalisation on the one hand, with the extremely important tools we all have in our hands, and on the other hand, the rules, the framework, the laws which protect people, because we want a people-centred development of digitalisation. this report identifies some of the key challenges that new technologies pose, indeed, to the world of work. addressing these challenges is all the more important in view of the effects of the covid-19 crisis, because this has accelerated a lot of these processes. in europe we can pride ourselves on a strong set of social and labour laws which already touch upon some of the challenges raised by this report. we have the working time directive, the occupational safety and health framework directive, the work-life balance directive and the transparent and predictable working conditions directive, to mention the ones which are relevant for remote working and have a direct impact on the ability of the worker to disconnect from work obligations. these laws protect the well-being of european workers and put forward safeguards, amongst other things, against excessive working hours and unpredictable work schedules, including for the ict-based work. we need to explore how best to seize the opportunities and address the challenges posed by digitalisation of the world of work, taking into account national industry and sectoral specificities, as the rapporteur has also mentioned. in this regard, the high-level conference on the future of work, remote work, challenges, risks and opportunities, planned by the portuguese presidency, comes very timely. implementing a right to disconnect is often a matter of finding the right balance between the nature of the tasks, management style, personal choices and company-level rules. certainly a one-size-fits-all approach is therefore not ideal, but this doesn’t diminish the importance of a right. then you have to implement the right according to the different situations, and certainly this can be best done through social dialogue. as rightly set out in your report, social partners have a central role in dealing with issues linked to this right to disconnect. social partners should take a leading role in this regard, and the commission stands ready to assist, ready to encourage. but this means that we have to be all de bonne foi. in the last few years, some member states have taken action by directly or indirectly mandating social partners to negotiate provisions on the right to disconnect. italy, spain, france, belgium are among those countries. and in the past, social partners have already agreed on a cross-industry framework agreement on telework, in 2002 – so quite a long time ago, when telework was starting. now telework is extending, and close to 30% and sometimes even more people are on telework. it would perhaps be important to have a look at this agreement and to adapt it to the present context and circumstances. social partners have also come together to agree on a more recent agreement on digitalisation, concluded in 2020. this framework agreement specifically tackles telework and modalities of connecting and disconnecting from work, and it is currently being implemented at national, regional and local level. in this specific field it is equally important to duly take into account the concerns on proportionality, subsidiarity and better law-making principles. all proposals for union action – and this is absolutely fundamental and applies also to the right to disconnect and eventually action in this field – must be subject, under article 154 of the treaty, to consultation with the eu’s social partners, who may decide to act by means of agreements, to act by negotiation between themselves. so anyway, this door is open – wide open. before deciding on any action on the right to disconnect, the commission certainly has to apply this article and will also discuss with social partners on these aspects. as a certain number of member states, as i recalled already, have already introduced a right to disconnect, many companies also establish this important right through agreements with their social partners, because they have understood what the rapporteur has described: people are not robots, people have limits. so, if you want to have better productivity, you cannot just occupy people 24 hours a day and seven days a week. so i think this is an important contribution, economic and social again, and this shows the importance of this right to disconnect for the good functioning of companies. and very often, by the way, it’s it companies who have introduced this right to disconnect. it underlines also the crucial role of social partners in this field. therefore, the commission is inviting social partners to proactively work together in order to come to an adequate solution for the benefit of workers and companies. certainly the commission is ready to accompany and support them in this endeavour, and then the right of the treaty – also of article 225 – is absolutely there and can be used by the commission if needed. (applause)

mr president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, it is important to remember that the right to disconnect applies to all workers and not just to those who are working remotely. and while there are many benefits to digitalisation in an employee's life, studies show that hyperconnectivity can lead to undesirable effects on work-life balance or well-being at work. we cannot accept that more and more workers are seeing their working hours increase without any additional income or compensatory rest. as a socialist, i welcome this report, which calls for the involvement of the social partners in the coming legislative process, but above all sets out the guidelines for the creation of such a right in europe, through a clear definition of the right to disconnect, the information of workers on their right to disconnect, the setting of new working conditions for online employment and the protection of workers against the risk of retaliation in the event of unavailability outside working hours. yes, european workers need the right to disconnect. let's make it happen!
mr president, telecommuting is a new way of working that is of interest to many employees but it can be felt as an unbearable constraint when it is imposed by a company, whether in normal times or during exceptional circumstances, such as the coronavirus pandemic. it is therefore useful to recognise the right of employees to disconnect, i.e. the right to take full advantage of their rest and leave without being disturbed by their employer. this is what the french law of 8 august 2016 did, this law recognizes this right to disconnect and wisely refers to the social dialogue to specify the modalities. this french example should inspire all the member states of the european union, because the union must not be content with being the europe of business, it must also have a social dimension. however, it is necessary to avoid imposing an unreasonable administrative burden on companies. furthermore, i consider that the creation of this new right of disconnection is a matter for the states and not for the union. for these two reasons, i am opposed to the adoption of a directive on this matter. let's trust the states.
mr president, i would like to thank you. during the coronavirus pandemic, many people are feeling the pressure to be available in their free time. we therefore propose to protect the right to take time off for all those who do not have a fixed working time. it is absolutely essential to me that the social partners draw up the agreement, and that does not have to be difficult. it is primarily a question of expectation voting. an agreement at a workplace for when and how to use e-mail and telephone. but not one so inflexible that you're not allowed to help if the whole thing goes up in flames. this is a small part of the road. there is still a long way to go if we are to help the many millions who suffer from stress. it is therefore essential that we have an ambitious strategy with a primary focus on health and safety at work. we must focus on this preventive action so that europe's workers can see that the work tasks are in line with working time and their skills, and that managers are better trained. there's no time to waste. let's get to it.
member of the commission. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i have listened to your speeches and i have not heard anyone who is opposed to this right to disconnect. why would you do that? because it's just common sense. as i have said and as others have also said, we cannot expect a person, however efficient, to be available at all times. you can demand it for a while, but if you go beyond the debate is closed. the vote on the amendments will take place today, wednesday, 20 january 2021. the final vote will take place on thursday 21 january 2021. written declarations (article 171) the following documents shall be submitted to the court of justice:
in writing. during the epidemic, as many as one third of all workers in the european union are working from home. it has its advantages, but it also has its disadvantages. the advantage is certainly less chance of spreading the coronavirus infection, and the downside is the feeling that the worker must be available at all times. working from home blurs the line between work and leisure. this is why the european parliament (on the initiative of s&d mep alex agius salibey) is advocating for the so-called right to disconnect, which means the right or the possibility for a worker to turn off his phone and e-mail after working hours, without fear of negative consequences. in the report, we call on the commission to make this right available to all workers in the eu. this will greatly reduce the pressure and increase the concern for the mental health of employees who have been facing an unpredictable situation and adapting to a new way of working for almost a year. this measure will also provide relief to many slovenians who are working remotely during the epidemic.
in writing. in times of social distancing and exit restrictions, work-life balance is very important and the right to check-out should be a right that is an integral part of work organisation in the new digital age. the measures taken in response to the covid-19 crisis have changed the way people work, demonstrating the importance of digital solutions. while working from home meant keeping a lot of jobs, 27% of those working from home reported doing work in their spare time. the spread of teleworking has put an even greater burden on young people and on those who have caring responsibilities, such as single parents, families with children or families caring for relatives. constant online contact, combined with a high volume of work tasks and the increasing expectation that employees are available at all times, can negatively affect the work-life balance, as well as their physical and mental health and well-being, and can lead to increased stress and burnout. the right to opt-out allows workers to refrain from work-related electronic communications, telephone calls and e-mails during rest periods or during leave without facing any disadvantages. respect for working time and its predictability are essential to ensure the health and safety of workers and their families in the union.
in writing. in order to adapt workers' rights to the changes brought about by homework, the european left has called for and initiated a european parliament report on the right to disconnect. the report is based on the impact of ict on working conditions faced by the majority of europeans forced by the covid-19 crisis to switch to a telework system. however, in addition to the positive aspects generated by this new system, such as the protection of jobs during the pandemic or greater flexibility in the management of the time, place and manner in which work is carried out, new challenges have emerged that present higher risks for workers and require coordination at the supranational level of the member states. according to eurofound, 27% of europeans who have worked from home say they have had to work in their spare time to fulfil their professional tasks. our proposal therefore addresses the right of this category of workers to disconnect and is based on recent studies that show us the importance of work-life balance on workers' physical and mental health, while protecting the flexibility so necessary for many workers today.

president-in-office of the council. – mr president, honourable members, i’ve listened carefully to the honourable mr tang. thank you for bringing this question to the plenary, as it is an important issue. the eu and its member states are committed to strengthening good tax governance, fair taxation, global tax transparency and the fight against tax fraud and evasion, both at eu level and globally. the ecofin council produced a set of conclusions on 27 november 2020 on fair and effective taxation. this provided political guidance on further work on a modern eu tax environment. these conclusions also express the council’s views on the commission tax action plan, issued in july 2020, on good tax governance in the eu and beyond. the council reiterated the importance of supporting the principles of good tax governance through the continuation of the successful work undertaken so far in the context of the code of conduct group, including the eu list of non-cooperative jurisdictions for tax purposes, which should be further pursued and enhanced where necessary. the council therefore requested that the code of conduct group continue its work. it also stressed the importance of fair treatment within the eu with respect to third countries and jurisdictions, while maintaining a continuous dialogue with third countries as well as with the oecd. the code of conduct group will also pursue its discussions on ways and means to further improve the work on the code. this should take into account the successful lessons from other experience gained so far. the eu list of non-cooperative jurisdictions for tax purposes was revised most recently in october 2020 following an in-depth review of the implementation of the commitments made by third countries’ jurisdictions that are part of the process. the next revision of the eu list, which is scheduled for february at the ecofin council, is prepared by the code of conduct group. as regards defensive measures towards non-cooperative jurisdictions for tax purposes, member states and the council adhere to a number of guiding principles. the defensive measures can have considerable consequences for the listed jurisdictions. the following aspects can be mentioned in this context. first, the key objective of the list is to ensure change, as mr tang said, and not punish the listed jurisdiction. being listed entails reputational damage and we see that this aspect tangibly contributes to the efficiency of the eu list. more and more jurisdictions change their practice and adopt tax good governance; standards that are also applicable between the eu member states. so, on the second aspect, a number of eu-level defensive measures are being applied vis-à-vis the listed jurisdictions, and these can have financial consequences. the work in this area is also continuing with the assistance of the commission. and third, member states are also free to apply national lists or defensive measures that go beyond what is agreed at the eu level or in the intergovernmental context of the code of conduct group. finally, it is important to recall that the measures agreed in 2017 in the council were reviewed in 2019 in the code of conduct group, and member states agreed to continue this work during this year. this reflects the fact that member states have different legal systems, different laws and it takes time to design new measures. work on defensive measures will not stop. coordination will continue, and it’s likely to increase in the near future. should the commission choose to table a legislative proposal in this area, it will of course be examined by the council in accordance with the treaty requirements and taking into account the limits of the eu’s competence in these matters.
member of the commission. – mr president, honourable members, first of all let me thank the committee on economic and monetary affairs (econ) and subcommittee on tax matters (fisc), and the rapporteur, mr tang, for putting the fight against tax evasion and tax avoidance at the forefront of the agenda. the eu list of non-cooperative jurisdictions will continue to play an important role in the years to come. and, i think, especially at this moment in time, in order to help overcome the economic and social crisis also caused by the pandemic, we have to strengthen these tools. the commission announced a commitment to work to strengthen these tools in july 2020, and this commitment will continue. of course, there is a need to improve tax good governance, not only globally, but also within the eu. member states are subject to reviews under various tools, and these tools include the code of conduct for business taxation, whose reform is an absolute priority, and infringement procedures in the areas directly covered by eu law. i count on the european parliament to continue pushing for an ambitious agenda. i am glad to hear the council’s commitment in this direction. the commission actively engaged with member states in the different council groups to discuss the follow-up to the communication on tax good governance in europe and beyond. as a result, the council adopted conclusions, as it was reminded, which take note of the communication and reiterate the importance of the principles of tax good governance and the need to enhance the eu listing process. this is an important step as it recognises that more work is needed. i have in mind, in particular, the revision of the code of conduct for business taxation. any change in this respect will have a major impact on the eu listing process. the progress on the discussions of minimally effective taxation in the context of pillar two of the oecd’s report are accordingly crucial for the code and, consequently, also for the eu listing process, and will have an effect on our fair taxation criterion, including zero-tax jurisdictions. the eu listing also requires improved administrative cooperation, in particular through the exchange of tax information. this is why the commission will continue to work on extending the eu list criteria to cover effective exchanges of information under the common reporting standard, country-by-country reporting between tax authorities and beneficial ownership information. i believe that it is also necessary that we focus on the right jurisdictions, and consider whether any relevant jurisdiction is missing from our radar. this is the reason why the commission is working on a revision of the scoreboard, and uses enhanced selection criteria for identifying jurisdictions and prioritising their screening under the eu listing process. the commission is also looking forward to assessing the actions undertaken by member states towards enacting domestic defensive measures vis-à-vis listed jurisdictions. i reiterate on this occasion that we are ready to take any necessary initiatives in case the results are not in line with our expectations, including by way of legislative proposal. finally, i believe that the council should report regularly to the parliament regarding its work on non-cooperative jurisdictions. this would improve the mutual understanding of the process and would help to focus on improving the eu listing process.

on behalf of the ecr group. – mr president, i would like to thank ms lagarde and mr dombrovskis for being here. in the context of the report we are discussing today, i would like to make four remarks and, of course, ask them some related questions. first of all, i think it’s more than fair to say that, given the circumstances that have fallen upon us, we are still in a very unusual situation with respect to the stance of monetary policy, with huge balance sheets increasing further by the day and negative nominal policy rates. a return to a more normal policy stance is, of course, not for tomorrow, not for next week, and probably not for next month either, but i think it would be good to be more explicit about the signposts that the path to normality will be. secondly, we see today unmistakeable signs of major bubbles in equity markets and other financial markets, all more or less linked to what i would call the overabundance of liquidity. these bubbles are a constant threat to financial stability, and by now we all know that financial stability is, of course, closely linked to price stability: the major objective of monetary policy in the euro area. i think it’s time to rethink the stance of monetary policy by taking these elements – bubbles, financial stability dangers – more explicitly into consideration. thirdly, thomas piketty and 150 other economists have called, very recently, for the cancellation of government debt by the ecb. i would be inclined to ask whether you share that opinion, but i think that is a superfluous question. but do you think the ecb statutes allow for such an action? fourthly, when a government crisis looms in a highly indebted country within the euro area, it always tends to make financial markets more nervous overnight, which – overnight – also tends to lead to increasing spreads. my question is: does the ecb consequently stand ready to intervene in such circumstances in order to keep these spreads down?

madam president, commissioner, the transition to the circular economy has the potential to create between 1.2 and 3 million new jobs by 2030! the list of actors involved is very long. for the circular economy to work, it needs a market. this market is the market for recycled raw materials. more specifically, it is to allow a plastic bottle manufacturer to use recycled plastic instead of plastic directly from oil. the reality is that there is currently not enough demand on the market for secondary raw materials produced from waste. it is therefore up to us to develop this by stimulating demand. first, by introducing mandatory recycled content in certain products. this will automatically create an increase in demand and thus opportunities for recycled raw materials. secondly, by guiding consumers' choices through clear and explicit labels on the design and recyclability of what they buy. in this way, they will change the market. despite the displeasure of some, the market economy can be a great opportunity to make a successful ecological transition.

in writing. in the context of the pandemic, millions of people have lacked access to education or training programmes, and the difficulties in adapting to the new digital context have widened the gap between and within member states. socioeconomic inequalities have made access to education increasingly difficult. the skills agenda for europe must be at the heart of european action so that the right to quality, lifelong training becomes a reality for all citizens, in all areas and sectors. in the context of the fact that 90% of jobs in the future will require digital skills, it is essential that the european institutions and the member states support the acquisition of new skills through european programmes and instruments such as erasmus+, the children and youth guarantee, the digital europe and creative europe programmes. the allocation of a minimum of 20% to digital transition in the recovery and resilience plans becomes essential and those resources need to be accompanied by appropriate measures and additional funds invested structurally by each member state. our investment in the skills of europeans today will dictate europe's competitiveness and economic performance in the future.

in writing. we all have a common interest in making europe's climate policy more effective, in promoting the green transition and in avoiding the risk of coal leakage. the mechanism for adjusting co2 emissions at the border can be useful in achieving these objectives. in order to contribute effectively to the objectives, the new instrument must meet three conditions. the new mechanism should have as its primary objective the protection of european businesses and industry. regulations are needed that make polluters, not people, pay for the consequences of harmful activities. it's the cornerstone of a just transition. it is also essential that the new mechanism is developed in the form of a structure that operates in parallel with the eu emissions trading system, complementing and strengthening existing instruments. the mechanism shall not affect the free allocation scheme. in order to avoid trade conflicts, the new instrument should be in line with the rules of the world trade organisation and with the international commitments of the european union. finally, due care and caution is required in the design of the mechanism. the european commission should therefore carry out thorough impact studies, broken down by industry, and consult industry stakeholders. a hasty regulation, pushed by the european left, would put hundreds of businesses and thousands of jobs at risk, which would have disastrous economic effects as well as undermine the social acceptance of the green transition.

author. madam president, commissioner dalli, i have the honour to take the floor to present the result of the joint work carried out as rapporteur for a motion for a resolution following an oral question from the committee on civil liberties, justice and home affairs, which i chair. the motion for a resolution deals with the rights of the child, the minor, the boy and the girl, the rights of the child, and does so in the light of the commission's imminent presentation of its eu strategy on the rights of the child. we expect that to be presented on 24 march, so that is exactly the time when we should review the contents of this resolution which is being put to the vote of the european parliament in this march plenary. it seeks to answer the six questions put to the commission concerning: national plans to implement the objectives set by the strategy; support for an inclusive and holistic approach that focuses in particular on the most vulnerable children; ensuring the participation of children as agents of change; the obligation of member states to provide adequate funding and, of course, the support of the commission; the mandatory link to the sustainable development goals and the united nations 2030 agenda; and taking into account the impact of the covid-19 pandemic, which has only exacerbated inequalities across the european union and in the member states. and that is why we are very conscious of the fact that the rights of the child are, for one thing, enshrined in the charter of fundamental rights of the european union, in a more explicit and powerful way than, surely, in any written constitution of any of the 27 member states of the union. it enshrines, first of all, the child's best interests, the principle which governs all protective law and which also inspires the child's correctional legislation. in the member states it is expressly enshrined. but it also contains, in addition to article 24, which enshrines the rights of the child, and article 21, which prohibits discrimination on grounds of age, an article 34 which, in an absolutely explicit and binding way, prohibits child labour and prohibits the exploitation of minors, guaranteeing in any case their access to the education system. the resolution which this parliament is about to vote on covers all these aspects in a text which is unusually long. there are twenty-seven recitals and forty paragraphs in the resolution, which take as their starting point the special problems of minors in the face of the fact of migration. we cannot ignore the fact that there are at least 200 million stateless children in search of a place of refuge, some of them in the european union, of course. there is also a link to the 2011 directive on combating sexual abuse and sexual exploitation of children and child pornography, which is binding for all member states, linked to the 2012 directive on the protection of victims, taking into account that many victims of sexual exploitation are indeed minors, who therefore require procedural treatment that should be guaranteed by the development by member states of the 2016 directive on procedural rights and access of minors to the exercise of all rights before the judicial system: the right to interpretation in a way that is understandable to them; the right to legal assistance and specialist assistance, and the protection of the best interests of the child in all proceedings. there is, as it should be, a concern expressed in the resolution about child poverty and a mandate to the european union to ensure, through a european plan we call the child poverty guarantee, that the needs of those 150 million poor children in the immediate vicinity of the european union and those 73 million children who are victims of sexual slavery and sexual exploitation are met. this morning we were discussing the european social pillar. we have every hope in the relaunch of the european pillar of social rights, but there will be no pillar if we are not able to include, as it deserves, the protection of the rights of minors and children, not only in the forthcoming strategy but also in the development legislation - the directives - because that development legislation which will follow the strategy will be the measure of the european parliament's commitment to the protection of minors and children.
vice-president of the commission. – madam president, dear members, thank you for your question in the context of our work on the upcoming european union strategy on the rights of the child. i have already engaged the honourable members on this, and i thank you for all your contributions. together with national authorities, we work to counter the negative consequences of the pandemic on children. this year my hope is that children everywhere will be able to return to school safely. hopes require actions, therefore, on 24 march, the commission will adopt its first–ever comprehensive european union strategy on the rights of the child. we want to achieve a child rights-based culture in our policy making. to answer your first question: member states are key partners. the strategy will contain concrete recommendations for action at member state level. member states’ representatives have been extensively consulted in our expert group. we are working with the current and future presidencies to facilitate member states’ endorsement of the strategy. we will also launch an european union network for children’s rights to facilitate mutual learning between member states, and to track the progress of action at national and european union level. in response to your second question on vulnerable children and non–discrimination, i must emphasise that children’s rights are universal. every child, regardless of background, gender, social, economic and residence status, should enjoy the same rights, the same life, free of discrimination. this will be the guiding principle of the strategy; targeted actions are envisaged under the thematic sections to address specific needs. regarding your question on the meaningful participation of children, i want to be very clear: not only is this a strategy for children, it is also a strategy developed with children. children are engaged citizens. more than 10 000 children were consulted in the preparation of the strategy and the child guarantee. this is unprecedented. we will also include children and young people in the deliberations of the conference on the future of europe. to answer your fourth question, the overall objective of the strategy will be to achieve the mainstreaming of child rights in all european union policies. for example, the digital decade communication includes child-specific principles. we are working on implementing the commission’s strategy to fight online child sexual abuse, the protection of children in our migration policy, and supporting child victims and children with cancer under the europe’s beating cancer plan, illustrate the necessity of this mainstreaming approach. the strategy will be adopted together with the proposal for a council recommendation on the european union child guarantee, which will tackle social exclusion, poverty and inequalities. you have asked about the funding. i’m particularly pleased with the agreement reached on the european social fund plus. at least five per cent of allocated money is earmarked for tackling child poverty under the child guarantee. increased investment in children means that member states must be encouraged to allocate european union funding for the implementation of the objectives and measures of the strategy. to answer, your fifth question, the strategy will be fully anchored in the european union charter of fundamental rights, in the european union convention on the rights of the child and it will also contribute to the sustainable development goals. the global dimension of child rights and protection will be addressed in a dedicated section. and your last question touches on the pandemic. every single thematic area of the strategy has been affected by the consequences of this pandemic, so we will leave no stone unturned in our bid to understand the full effects on children’s health, development and well–being. thank you for listening, and i’m also ready to listen to your views now.

in writing. children's rights are an integral part of the human rights that the european union is obliged to respect under the un convention on the rights of the child, which poland initiated over 40 years ago. unfortunately, many of the problems of child protection remain unresolved and we are now seeing new ones emerge. the covid-19 pandemic has presented member states and the european union with a number of different challenges. the move to online learning has shown the scale of digital exclusion, and many schools have failed to organize classes. the additional effect was that the children developed mental and psychological problems, loneliness, and even depression, associated with the limitation of peer contact. many families have lost at least part of their income, which has directly affected the situation and financial security of their children. in addition, there is a risk of an increase in violence against children, both domestic violence where the perpetrators cannot be isolated and online violence, as a significant part of the activity is transferred to the network.
in writing. the protection of the rights and best interests of the child is explicitly enshrined in the european charter of fundamental rights and in article 3 of the eu treaty. in the light of the new european strategy on the rights of the child, we regret to see that children are still victims of violence, exploitation, abuse, discrimination, poverty and social exclusion. among other things, the pandemic has created new challenges, brought to light incidents of domestic violence against minors and highlighted the modern pathology of exposing millions of children to the dangers of the internet. just consider that before the pandemic, one in four children in europe was at risk of poverty, a figure that is expected to double. cyberbullying has skyrocketed, and the majority of children have been victimized by people they trusted. in this context, it must not be forgotten that children are by definition the most vulnerable groups in the population and all policies concerning them must take account of their special needs according to their age. we welcome the new european strategy and call on the commission to guarantee all children inclusive access to education and to put the best interests of children at the heart of any relevant legislative initiative.
the next item is the debate on the statements by the council and the commission on the reform of the eu policy framework to end tax avoidance in the eu following the openlux revelations (2021/2558 ((rsp)).
president-in-office of the council. – mr president, thank you for the opportunity to contribute to this discussion. the challenges of european taxation constitutes one of our presidency priorities, establishing a fair and efficient model of taxation, strengthening of good governance mechanisms, the global tax transparency, and to stepping up the fight against tax fraud, evasion and avoidance through non-cooperative jurisdiction are some of the areas where we want to advance. as you are aware, it was under the portuguese presidency that the dossier on the country-by-country report (cbcr) has advanced substantially in the council. over the last few years, the council has achieved a lot by extending the scope of administrative cooperation in taxation matters, most recently also to digital platforms. tax rulings issued to companies will not be a secret any more. tax authorities can now exchange information on country-by-country reports and potentially aggressive cross-border tax planning schemes. administrative cooperation in the area of vat is also taking a much higher level. in the context of enhanced transparency, it is also worth mentioning recent and planned improvements in the area of anti-money laundering framework, including on determining beneficial ownership, a key aspect of the openlux investigation. and, of course, there is the anti-tax avoidance directive, which provides a comprehensive framework of anti-abuse measures so that taxation occurs where value is created. as regards the openlux specifically, allow me to underline some points. first, the eu has a set of clearly-defined competences in the treaties where certain matters are left to national competence. this means that we have to look into what each of the other member states is doing so that the sovereign right of one country doesn’t limit the sovereign right of the others. secondly, the commission is doing what is necessary, either through legislative proposals through well-established procedures to ensure the full compliance of all member states with eu law under equal conditions. we all have to act within the limits of our own competences. as far as the competences of the council are concerned, the presidency will continue to work on this matter, building on the political guidance of the council conclusions on fair and effective taxation in times of recovery, on tax challenges linked to digitalisation and on tax good governance in the eu and beyond, which the council approved last november. these conclusions touched also on international cooperation, which is an element of the parliament’s resolution on reforming the eu list of tax havens. global cooperation is key to combating base erosion and profit-shifting. allow me to cite two well-known examples. first, the code of conduct group. with the eu list of non-cooperative jurisdictions, member states have contributed to changing a considerable number of harmful tax practices in third countries. most of the more than 90 jurisdictions have aligned themselves with the standards common to the eu member states, and this is in itself an achievement. member states have also achieved a lot in the area of intergovernmental corporate tax policy coordination within the eu. the eu conduct group examines existing laws, establishes practices in eu countries which affect, or may affect in a significant way, the location of business activity in the eu and the group is regularly looking into further improving its functioning on the basis of its achievements. a second example is the digitalised economy. the digitalised economy enables structures that shift profits to entities that are taxed at a very low rate or not at all. the member states are working closely with the oecd to find a global solution that covers both the allocation of taxing rights and anti—profit shifting rules. we are doing everything we can to reach an agreement by mid-2021. both the council and the european council will discuss these matters in march. to conclude, i believe that, not least in the context of the pandemic, we should continue to explore avenues for adjusting the eu policy framework for combating tax avoidance. i’m convinced that the council and member states will swiftly make further progress in the area of taxation, and the contribution of the european parliament to this endeavour will be of the highest value for this discussion.
member of the commission. – mr president, press investigations and public disclosures have been a great propeller of positive change by exposing weaknesses to the public and creating political momentum for the european parliament and the european institutions to act. thanks to openlux, we know more than before on issues concerning the implementation of anti-money laundering rules and transparency of beneficial ownership information, on the use of aggressive tax planning strategies, and on the existence of companies with no or very little economic substance, the so-called shell companies. openlux points to problems which, by nature, have no borders. we need eu solutions. the aim to increase transparency of information is a key driver for the commission agenda. after the fifth anti-money laundering directive, which by the way enabled the openlux investigation, a step forward in transparency will be achieved soon with the interconnection of a system of national registers, which will allow national competent authorities to have direct access to information held by the national registers of the other member states. other very important steps have been achieved, thanks to the two anti-tax avoidance directives and the dac 6 on the mandatory disclosure of potentially aggressive cross-border tax arrangements. as a result, the eu today has a legislative framework in place that makes it the frontrunner on standards of transparency and anti-avoidance rules, compared to other global players. however, we cannot be complacent. while national governments are struggling to face revenue needs, a decisive step up to ensure more effective eu-wide compliance with the principle of progressive tax is needed. it would support redistribution and reduction of inequalities among our economies. moreover, we also need improvements to the eu list of non-cooperative jurisdictions, as we discussed here last month with a resolution of the parliament. first, we have to make sure that all the rules we have adopted at the eu level are effectively enforced by all member states. second, we need to constantly work to further strengthen our legal tools to curb illicit behaviours. the openlux investigation revealed that a large number of companies have failed to meet their reporting obligations. this is a matter of monitoring and, of course, it is not acceptable, neither in the case of luxembourg nor or any other eu member states. we have eu rules and all eu member states have to follow them. in addition, in an ever-evolving world, tax practices continuously evolve as well. this is why clamping down on tax avoidance and tax fraud remains high on our political agenda. in july last year, the commission tabled an action plan for fair and simple taxation, which now has to be put in practice, and we will not stop there. the commission services are working intensively on additional proposals, including on the fight against tax avoidance and on the public disclosure of certain information about income tax by large undertakings. we intend to provide more detail on some of those initiatives in the forthcoming communication on business taxation. let me briefly speak about some of them. first, shell companies – entities with no or very little economic substance – can pose a real threat within the internal market in terms of tax base erosion and profit shifting, and they also play a role in transactions linked to money laundering and tax evasion. my services are currently reflecting on an additional amendment to the anti-tax avoidance directive as soon as possible, in order to tackle the challenges linked to the use of shell companies in relation to tax avoidance. as regards the fight against aggressive tax planning, it is worth mentioning two parallel initiatives: the reform of the mandate of the code of conduct of the business taxation group and the recovery and resilience facility. the reform of the code of conduct mandate aims at broadening the scope to assess and ensure the proper monitoring and assessment of all relevant tax measures in member states. the recovery and resilience facility context, the member states concerned by a recommendation on aggressive tax planning are currently submitting to the commission their national plans. due consideration will be given to tax reforms aimed at decisive steps against aggressive tax planning strategies o foster corporate transparency. i am pleased to see the recent unblocking in the council on the proposal for a directive on country—by—country reporting, and i congratulate the portuguese presidency for this step forward. parliament and the council will hopefully soon start the trilogues and finalise the negotiations. honourable members, action only within the eu would not be sufficient, as shown in the openlux investigation, their potential harmfulness seems to have been exacerbated when complemented with reduced transparency in third countries, especially those with no income tax or with significant deficiencies in their anti-money laundering or tax transparency frameworks. this is why tackling the international dimension of the beneficial ownership—related deficiencies is one of the priorities for the future of the eu list. we need to integrate, effectively, beneficial ownership within the eu listing process. last but not least, a few words on minimum effective taxation to put a floor to tax competition. i only see two possible scenarios. if an agreement is reached at the oecd on pillar 2 within the timeline that we have, this will be transposed into eu law. if no agreement is reached at the oecd, the commission is committed to taking eu action to ensure a minimum level of effective taxation, taking into account the landing point of the current global discussions.
