the next item is the report by mr antonius manders, on behalf of the committee on legal affairs and citizens' rights, on the report on the liability of undertakings for environmental damage (2020/2027 (ini)) (a9-0112/2021).
- i'm the reporter. mr president, commissioner, 20 years ago i was the rapporteur for the environmental liability directive. this directive has not yet been fully transposed into national law by all member states, leading to divergent enforcement of liability legislation. we have drawn up an own-initiative report with a number of recommendations to the european commission and the council which ideally should be incorporated in a regulation to ensure that the rules are fully harmonised and can be enforced in the same way throughout the union. this will create a level playing field for businesses and protect the environment. the first objective of this legislation is to prevent accidents. after all, no one benefits from it if there is damage to be repaired that could have been prevented. we therefore urge the commission, and especially the member states, to review the existing directive, which has basically never worked or has not worked well enough. twenty years ago, no one knew about pfas and genx. the world is not standing still. on the one hand we are talking about artificial intelligence and on the other hand we want to protect the environment with legislation that is 20 years old and is still being rejected by the member states. we started this owninitiative report with 180 different amendments and, with the support of all our colleagues and the coordinators of the various groups, we have succeeded in reaching a unanimous position. i think that is a very good proposal. i would like to thank, among others, the adviser to our group, julia lindemann, and my colleague marijn verhees, who have done a great deal of work. i would like to explain some of the recommendations. the current environmental liability directive has been transposed differently by all member states and its supervision is also very different. we need to get rid of that. we need a fully harmonised legislative proposal to create an internal market which can act as a lever with other countries and lift european industry to a high level. we are therefore expressly in favour of the reciprocity of legislation that we know here, or commissioner reynders' due diligence, being imposed on third countries so that we can export european standards and values to these countries and protect european industry from cheap companies from other countries that overstep the law. furthermore, the existing definitions are unclear. the technology is not at a standstill, which means that the definitions must also be updated. i would also like to draw attention to the access of interested parties to justice. we refer explicitly to the aarhus convention in the proposal because we believe that the rules should be interwoven. it is not possible that we have the aarhus convention on the one hand and do not have access to justice on the other. the commission is also proposing to set up a european task force to help member states implement the future legislation properly, to exchange information on the situation in other countries and to assist member states in properly enforcing the legislation. we are also introducing compulsory insurance for companies in different categories to ensure that the taxpayer does not have to pay for the pollution caused by companies. we also want to introduce chain liability, so that there is no small legal entity that causes damage and then goes bankrupt or cannot be traced and the taxpayer is responsible for the damage. for example, 20 years ago a subsidiary of pfizer was marketing contaminated sugar water. the company had caused a lot of damage which could not be recovered from anyone because it was not clear whether the matter was covered by national or eu law. so did chemours, which dumped pfas and genx in a landfill in italy and then washed its hands in innocence because it had processed so-called waste. this will no longer be possible thanks to chain liability. it is important to us that the directors of large companies who deliberately damage the environment for profit should also be held personally liable. the commission has already taken steps to ensure that the directive is implemented. the proposal places particular emphasis on prevention. we hope that the commission will translate this proposal into a regulation and that the member states will not only think of the short-term national interest, but also of the interests of our children and grandchildren and of the future of the european union. finally, we believe that the definition of the term 'ecocide' should be left to international organisations and then be taken over by the eu.
member of the commission. – mr president, let me first of all thank the rapporteur, mr manders, the shadow rapporteurs and the committee on legal affairs (juri) for the excellent work on this important report. thanks also, of course, go to the committee on the environment, public health and food safety (envi), the committee on civil liberties, justice and home affairs (libe), and the committee on development (deve) that have provided their opinions on this matter. environmental crime is growing. it causes serious harm to the environment, to human health and law—abiding companies. preventing and remedying environmental damage, but also ensuring that conduct endangering or damaging the environment are criminalised, are both necessary for a greener and more sustainable europe. the environmental crime and environmental liability directives are complementary in that respect, and this is also reflected in your report, which broadly addresses a basic challenge that has been around since human societies first enacted laws – namely what do we do when laws are disregarded and harm is caused? when it comes to europe’s environmental laws, half-hearted enforcement and poor accountability are the weakest links in the chain. in a market economy, much of our prosperity depends on companies. most will comply with our laws, but from experience we all know that some will infringe those laws and cause environmental harm. europe has a number of legal instruments in place to deal with this kind of behaviour. the report focuses on two in particular: the environmental liability directive and the environmental crime directive. it also focuses on a range of related topics. as you know, we are in the process of preparing a revision of the environmental crime directive under the lead of my colleague didier reynders, but our actions do not stop there. we also have a framework for cooperating with national inspectors, police prosecutors and judges, for instance, and under my own lead we will soon start an evaluation of the environmental liability directive. your input into our work is most useful and appreciated, and it is timely. i can assure you that we will consider the european parliament’s report very carefully, and we look forward to continuing constructive cooperation on all the topics covered by the report and to delivering the level of accountability that our citizens and our environment deserve.

president-in-office of the council. – mr president, i would like to thank the commissioner and honourable members for this debate on data protection adequacy. the council believes that the eu must find the best solution to make the transfer of personal data possible to a european economic area third country, territory or international organisation, while at the same time respecting eu legislation and case-law. when the conditions are fulfilled, adequacy decisions should be adopted. this is in line with the european council conclusions of october 2020, in which the heads of state or government welcomed the european strategy for data. this strategy supports the european union’s global digital ambition to build a true european competitive data economy while ensuring values and a high level of data security, data protection and privacy. as you know, the council itself does not take part in the adoption of adequacy decisions, although member states are involved in the comitology procedures. this being said, let’s look at the transfer of personal data to the uk. according to the commission explanations provided in the draft decision, the uk has chosen to keep its data protection framework fully aligned with the eu rules. the uk has strong safeguards in the area of government access to data and therefore provides an equivalent to data protection. these elements are essential, both to safeguard economic activity and to maintain a high level of cooperation with the uk in different sectors, including law—enforcement cooperation. the trade and cooperation agreement (tca) provides for a maximum of six months during which the uk is not to be considered a third country for the purpose of transferring personal data, and, as you know, this period expires at the end of june. after the draft adequacy decisions have been presented by the commission and the european data protection board provides its opinion, the process of adopting the adequacy decisions should be completed in time to make sure that there is a solid legal base for the transfer of personal data with the uk. so, we will continue to support the commission to come up with solutions that at the same time respect the fundamental rights of the union and the tca timeframe. that is essential, both to safeguard economic activity, in particular for smes and startups, and to maintain a high level of cooperation with the uk in different sectors, including law enforcement, as i said, and judicial cooperation. the uk will continue to be a very important partner of the european union in these areas. besides, adequacy decisions are not the end of the story – it is always important to keep an eye on evolution in the third state concerned, and the adequacy decisions provide for such a mechanism, in addition to the well—known sunset clause. this is also an important safeguard as it is important to make sure that the uk maintains a high level of protection of personal data in the future, and, if there are problematic divergences, this will certainly have consequences. now let’s talk about the transfer of personal data to the united states. turning to this point, it is clear that the invalidation of the privacy shield by the european court of justice has important implications, even if the court upheld the validity of the standard contractual clauses. these standard contractual clauses for the transfer of personal data will soon be updated, and they play an important role by providing additional legal certainty. we are confident that negotiations will intensify, following the joint statement by commissioner reynders and the us secretary of commerce, gina raimondo, of 25 march. the council and the member states are following these negotiations closely on the basis of information provided by the commission and i look forward to hearing commissioner reynders speak on this topic.
member of the commission. – mr president, i am grateful for the opportunity to discuss with you all this morning two important draft resolutions of this parliament: a first one on the consequences and lessons of the schrems ii judgment and a second one on the uk draft adequacy decisions. on 16 july last year, the european court of justice invalidated the eu-us privacy shield, concluding that insufficient protections were in place on the us side. the schrems ii ruling is a strong reaffirmation of the fundamental right to data protection under eu law. the court confirmed that protection must travel with data, and that the level of this protection must meet eu standards. in this ruling, the court also provided us with precise requirements that need to be fulfilled when adopting adequacy decisions, such as the ones we have proposed with respect to the uk, and the one we are discussing with the us, in view of a possible successor to the privacy shield. this being said, the two resolutions that we are discussing today concern two situations that are very different. the one concerning the draft uk adequacy decisions is about managing and remedying possible future divergence, since the uk data protection rules are currently aligned with the eu ones. in contrast, the other resolution is about building convergence with important international partners, such as the us, through the development of additional and strong data protection safeguards. complying with eu law standards, including the case-law of the eu court of justice, calls, in particular, for the delicate balance between national security and privacy to be addressed. this is not an easy balance to strike. as the commissioner responsible for both the rule of law and the protection of personal data, it is my responsibility and my personal commitment to ensure full compliance with all the elements of the judgment of our highest court. let me now briefly turn to each of the two resolutions. let me first address the draft adequacy decisions relating to the united kingdom. less than three weeks ago, an overwhelming majority in this plenary voted to approve the eu-uk trade and cooperation agreement (tca) by 660 votes in favour. data protection standards were not subject to negotiation with the uk. in fact, the tca provides that transfers of data to be carried out in the context of its implementation will need to take place in compliance with the requirements of the laws of the transferring party (which means, for the eu, the general data protection regulation (gdpr) and the law enforcement directive (led)). in this context, the eu’s interest is that the many transfers that will necessarily take place in application of the tca, in a wide range of areas, from trade to law-enforcement cooperation, will be based on a comprehensive instrument, requiring a high level of protection. such an instrument should also allow us to react if this level of protection is undermined. this is what our draft adequacy decisions provide for. first, they recognise that today the uk system continues to be based on the same rules that were applicable when the uk was a member state of the eu. this is the result of a deliberate choice of the uk legislator, which has decided to fully incorporate the principles, rights and obligations of the gdpr and the law enforcement directive into the british post-brexit legal system. it is difficult to find a system that is more equivalent to ours. in addition, the uk shares with eu member states a number of international commitments in the area of data protection, be it under the european convention on human rights, as interpreted by the european court of human rights, or the specific treaty on data protection of the council of europe. this is particularly important as regards the balance between national security and privacy: it means that also in that area, the uk adheres to the same standards as the eu member states. this is why we have made very clear in our draft decisions that adherence to such international instruments is a central element of an adequacy finding. second, recognising the current alignment between the uk and the eu does not mean that we are naïve or unprepared. we fully share parliament’s concerns on the possible future evolution of the uk system. brexit means that the uk data protection system will be administrated in a fully autonomous way. even very similar rules can be interpreted, applied or enforced differently. the key question is therefore, in our view, whether we can trust the uk not to lower the current level of protection. the commission is aware of the scepticism of a number of members of this parliament towards the uk in this regard. as president von der leyen said of our new relationship with the uk, ‘trust is good, but law is better’. this is why we have significantly reinforced certain important aspects of our approach on adequacy compared to previous decisions concerning other third countries. in particular, our proposed decisions – for the first time – strictly limit the duration of the adequacy findings by including a sunset clause: the decisions will automatically expire four years after their entry into force. if we were to consider that our adequacy findings can be renewed because the uk continues to ensure an adequate level of data protection, this will need to be subject to new decisions. such decisions will have to be adopted following the entire adequacy decision-making process, with an opinion of the european data protection board and a comitology procedure. by including that time limitation, we make clear towards the uk that possible problematic divergences will have consequences. this comes on top of – and does not replace – other mechanisms that we have also reinforced, and that would allow us to react immediately at any time, without waiting for the four year-period to expire if changes are introduced in uk law, or if there are practices that would undermine the level of protection. i am thinking of the suspension and termination mechanisms provided for in our draft decisions, in addition to the sunset clause. following the receipt in april of the opinion of the european data protection board (edpb), which was largely in agreement with the commission’s approach, we have further strengthened these mechanisms by identifying even more clearly in the draft decisions the aspects requiring specific monitoring and for which, in the event of divergence, we would trigger the suspension or termination procedure that we had already provided for in the initial draft. this concerns, for instance, the way the uk will implement its rules on international transfers. more generally, following the edpb’s opinion, we have clarified our decisions on a number of aspects regarding both, firstly, why we consider that today the uk ensures an adequate level of protection, and, secondly, how we intend to react if the situation changes. this includes aspects that i know are particularly important for this parliament, and that are discussed in the draft resolution: from certain possible limitations to some data protection rights for other objectives of public interest, such as immigration control, to the conditions, limitations and safeguards that apply in the event that national security authorities seek access to data. once again, we believe that we can credibly address the uncertainties of the future while recognising that the starting point is an adequate one at this stage. in particular, the sunset clause sends the message to the uk that problematic divergence will have a cost. however, it will only have its intended dissuasive effect if we clearly distinguish, on the one hand, convergence – and its benefits from, on the other hand, divergence – and its risks and consequences. to sum up, based on our assessment, after having taken into account the opinion of the edpb, as well as concerns raised by this parliament and by the member states, the commission is of the view that, as things stand, at this stage, we should go ahead with the adequacy decisions. let me now turn to the second issue of today’s debate. in response to some of the points raised in the second draft resolution, i would like to update you on what the commission is doing following the schrems ii judgment. first, we are finalising the modernisation of standard contractual clauses for international data transfers that fully take into account the requirements of the schrems ii judgment. we are very close to final adoption, which will probably take place in the next weeks, after a successful conclusion of a comitology procedure. as standard contractual clauses are the most-used tool by european companies for their international data transfers, this is a top priority for us. we have revised the clauses on the basis of the feedback received from the european data protection board and the european data protection supervisor. we have also taken into account the input we received from stakeholders during a broad public consultation. the new clauses will provide companies with a practical toolbox to assist them in their compliance efforts. because they are a ready-made tool, they will be particularly useful for smes, which, as is also pointed out in the draft resolution, may have limited resources and expertise. in addition, we will be in consultation with stakeholders to develop a user—friendly practical guide on the basis of questions and answers to further facilitate the use of these new standard contractual clauses. i also fully agree on the importance, stressed in your resolution, of ensuring consistency between the standard contractual clauses and the guidance of the european data protection board on schrems ii, which is currently being finalised after a public consultation. that is why, in revising the draft standard contractual clauses, we have worked very closely with the board to align our approaches and to provide companies with legal certainty. finally, we are also working with the us on a possible successor arrangement to the privacy shield. what is certainly positive is that we see real engagement from the administration of president biden, and a clear willingness to work on possible solutions. this was also reflected in my recent statement with the us secretary of commerce gina raimondo, with whom i have been in contact on a regular basis since she took office. at the same time, we also have to recognise that the issues around access to data for national security purposes that have to be addressed are very complex. as like-minded partners, the eu and the us should be able to find appropriate solutions on fundamental principles, such as access to a court, enforceable individual rights, and safeguards against excessive interferences with privacy. but let me be clear: there are no shortcuts and there will be no quick fix. we will only accept a solution that is fully in line with the requirements of union law, as interpreted by the court of justice. this is a question of compliance with the decision of our highest court. it is also in the mutual interest of the eu and the us that we put in place a solid, sustainable and legally certain transatlantic transfer mechanism. i know i can count on your support and the support of the entire parliament for solutions based on strong safeguards, which can, in that way, facilitate transfers. so i will continue to work and discuss this matter with the us in such a way, and i thank you for your attention this morning on those two very important topics and i am now looking forward to our debate.

mr president, in presenting the union's industrial strategy, the european commission is inviting us to think economically. it is time to ask the question of the handicaps you impose on our companies: the inflation of standards, some of which are absurd, the distorted competition, i am thinking in particular of posted workers, the impossibility of access to public contracts for our smes. you call it digital and green transition. on the digital transition, we can only say "finally!" europe has seen the digital revolution elude it because of your bureaucratic inertia. it was the americans and the chinese who made a decisive breakthrough. on the ecological transition, beware of the temptation that underlies your approach, that of punitive ecology. the great revolutions - and the ecological revolution is one of them - are only made by adherence and not by coercion, by positive collaboration and not by forced enlistment. the coercive cultural revolution, that's mao tse-tung, that comes from totalitarianism and it doesn't work. so use incentive more than repression. this ecological reflection also requires you to revise your globalist software, the one that programs, for example, the specialization of the regions of the world by type of activity. china, the world's factory? that's a good idea. we saw what this has done during covid: the shortage for our countries, the humiliation of a europe that cannot produce paper masks. today, to be close is to be ecologically virtuous and that means being penalized. it means being forced to comply with overwhelming environmental or social standards and being competed with by countries that are not bound by any rules. the ecological revolution we are calling for is the localist revolution: the one that turns its back on free trade agreements in favour of fair trade agreements that allow for controlled and virtuous trade. the localist revolution means implementing short circuits everywhere to produce, consume and recycle locally. the keyword should no longer be mobility, but proximity.

in writing. small and medium-sized enterprises (smes) account for around 100 million jobs and more than 50% of gdp in the european union. the survival of smes, family businesses and individual entrepreneurs is the key to the functioning of the european economy. it is therefore of the utmost importance that smes receive effective assistance while curbing the coronavirus pandemic. successful action depends on three factors: reducing red tape, providing additional resources and respecting the rights of others. it is good that the european commission has also recognised the importance of reducing the bureaucratic burden on smes. in the current situation, it would be irresponsible to burden smes with the ideological expectations of the european left. therefore, efforts to put the principle of 'one country, one vote' into practice are welcome. however, in parallel with the reduction of red tape, there is a need to expand subsidies and programmes for smes. neither the revised industrial policy strategy nor the commission's statements so far have adequately addressed these issues. developed programmes and targeted resources are needed to effectively support the digital and green transition of smes. finally, the european commission must give due respect to smes. it is incomprehensible that, a year and a half after taking office, the commission has been unable to define the tasks and powers of the eu sme pillar. the commission has also proposed that the european parliament and the council adopt a decision on the establishment of a european agency for the evaluation of medicinal products for human use (hereinafter 'the agency'), which will be responsible for the evaluation of medicinal products for human use.
in writing. small and medium-sized enterprises across the european union have been severely affected by the pandemic. the commission has also received comments from the united kingdom, the united kingdom and the united states on the application of the union state aid rules to the measures in question. this situation shows us once again the fragility of the european economic environment and the risks faced by smes in the eu. unfortunately, the impact of the pandemic has been felt strongly at the level of small entrepreneurs, and many companies with capital difficulties have reduced their activity or even gone bankrupt. this is unfortunately the case in romania, where most smes are unbankable and have had to consume their last resources to survive. moreover, in the absence of coherent support measures from the right-wing government of romania, some of the companies have ceased their activity or have preferred to increase prices. the solution can come from the european union, both through appropriate regulation and through support mechanisms through recovery plans. unfortunately, some countries, including romania, have ignored the call of smes. let's not forget the small entrepreneurs and find together solutions to save the european local economy!
in writing. studies show that recovery from the crisis will take years, and for some sectors, a return to pre-pandemic levels is not expected until 2024. additionally, these cautious forecasts are conditioned by references to the fact that the rate of recovery also depends on the effects of the vaccination campaign, the epidemiological situation, national policies, the ability of business to adopt. delayed or unrecorded effects of the epidemic should be taken into account, which may also play a negative role. however, smes have been the most affected by the crisis, including the problem of payment bottlenecks. many of these are now referred to by experts as "phantom companies", meaning those that have effectively ceased operations and exist only with the help of national pandemic support measures that are set to end in the fall. however, smes play a very important role, inter alia in strategic sectors, where they dominate the second and third tier supplier segment. there is therefore a risk that they will be adopted by non-european actors, which will create problems for the security of individual member states as well as the security of the union. therefore, both at national and union level, strategic segments should be monitored, inter alia, for the status of their european smes in order to ensure that their role in value chains is preserved.
in writing. – beyond the steep drop in their value added, jobs provided by smes decreased by more than 1.4 million in the past year of covid-19 crisis. yet the systemic handicaps smes face on a european scale stretch farther than the pandemic. thus, on average, the costs to comply with new rules are 10 times higher relatively for small businesses than they are for large enterprises. when new legislation is being mooted, like in the digital area, we all stress the need for regulations to maintain proportionality. in practice, new rules are being designed for the larger enterprises, and then get scaled down for smes. inherently, this means that rules carry a bias against small size, which should be continually kept in mind by legislation-makers. applying the rules should not hinder smes’ capacity to grow and create jobs. more and more new rules are being needed to address a wide variety of global challenges from climate change to technological innovation. inbuilt in the design of such legislation must remain the priority of helping smes become more resilient in the face of ongoing challenges while minimising, simplifying and streamlining administrative requirements. i welcome the fact that the european union seems to be applying more thoroughly its ‘think small first’ principle.
in writing. small and medium-sized enterprises (smes) were the most affected by the closures. the measures taken so far deserve reflection and i believe that the time has come to think of bold initiatives to revive this sector. one of the main obstacles faced by italian smes on a daily basis is bureaucracy, and that is why simplification and streamlining of procedures is crucial in my view. as regards regulatory requirements, greater flexibility should have been provided, especially for disposals affecting the credit environment of the real economy and smes, in order to reduce the impact on banks' balance sheets. another very divisive issue to consider is climate and the environment. as i have said many times before, we are running the great risk of setting our companies such ambitious targets that they are unrealistic in practical terms. a concrete and current example is the directive on single-use plastics, which is threatening the jobs of thousands of european citizens. for these reasons, i expect a concrete and effective response from the institutions, which will be able to revive this sector, which is so important to the economy.

executive vice-president of the commission. – madam president, i would very much like to begin by thanking the rapporteur, johan van overtveldt, and all the shadow rapporteurs for their comprehensive report. i think it provides an excellent basis for today’s debate. i think this engagement deserves our warm thanks. the time and effort put into this report show the parliament’s interest in competition policy and how this is seen as an important policy area. that’s because it goes to the very heart of the choices we need to make for europe to recover from the pandemic. we need to recover in a way that is strong and sustainable, and of course to continue to offer europeans what they deserve: societies that include them and provide for them. this is also a europe that seizes the opportunity that comes with the green and digital transitions that give companies of all sizes a fair chance to compete on their merits on a level playing field, to the benefit of the businesses themselves and obviously for us as consumers. the past 15 months have put a strain on every individual, every human that lives on this planet. our societies and our economies have been under great strain and, as it happens, it has shown the importance of well—functioning markets for things to continue, for value chains to deliver, for goods to be brought to supermarkets, for hospital equipment to be available, and for protective gear to be there. competition policy is essential to reach that goal. the passing months have also shown that our rules remain relevant, that they serve us well and that they can be swiftly adapted if need be. when the crisis hit, our state aid rules enabled quick and effective support to address the economic consequences of covid—19, while at the same time maintaining the integrity of the single market. the state aid temporary framework enabled member states to make use of the full flexibility of rules to support their businesses. since march 2020 the commission has adopted more than 500 decisions and approved over eur 3 trillion in aid. the temporary framework is currently set to apply until the end of this year. we continue to monitor its ability to offer the necessary support, especially for those sectors that are hardest hit, and we know that has everything to do with humans travelling, sleeping, eating – in short, hospitality, culture, tourism. we will continue to look at it because obviously it is important that we can still give support where the crisis has hit, while progressively phasing out the crisis rule once the situation allows for it. but this year we have not only dealt with the crisis. along with keeping up the pace of our enforcement, we have worked to ensure that our competition rule book remains fit for the challenges, including those from the green and digital transition. we have launched a reflection process on how competition rules can contribute to the objective of the european green deal, and indeed we did it in the parliament. we are now in the process of reviewing key state aid rules to ensure that they are fully fit for purpose. just today, we have launched a public consultation on the new climate, energy and environmental state aid guidelines. they will play a key role in enabling the green transition, while maintaining a level playing field in the single market. we also looked at the jurisdictional and procedural aspects of our merger rules, and we have issued new guidance on the application of the referral mechanism by member states to the eu level, to work very closely with national competition authorities to enable us to review what we sometimes call killer acquisitions, including in digital markets, things that would otherwise go unnoticed. we are revising our market definition notice to take stock of developments, and also, of course, revising our vertical and horizontal block exemption regulation. so it is indeed a busy year. looking forward, not only do we look at competition rules as such, and not only do we enforce them vigorously, but we also seek regulatory solutions to address systemic behaviours arising on large digital platforms with a gatekeeping role. in december last year, we adopted the digital markets act proposal. it aims to ensure that digital markets within our union remain open and contestable so that companies, both large and small, have fair opportunities to compete online, as they do offline. the digital markets act will tell the very large gatekeepers what to do and indeed what not to do. it will enable us, in close cooperation with national competition authorities, to act and to sanction gatekeepers who do not respect the rules. the proposal has progressed very well in council, and i am very happy to see how the pace is picking up in parliament. i really appreciate that engagement and that interest because we need the regulation and we need it fast. i very much look forward to continuing the discussion with parliament’s committees and members over the coming months. last, but not least, in addition we’ve just tabled a proposal to deal with foreign subsidies because they can be very distortive. as you will know by heart, for 60 years our state aid rules have been ensuring that aid granted by member states is targeted, proportional and does not undermine fair competition in the single market. but similar rules for subsidies do not exist for subsidies granted by foreign states, so our proposal aims to make this imbalance a thing of the past. companies that receive subsidies from non—eu countries will need our approval before they implement big mergers in europe, in addition to clearance under the eu merger regulation. companies will have to tell us what subsidies they have received when they bid in large public tenders and, again, won’t be able to win and to close those tenders without our ok. we’ll have the power on our own initiative to investigate any company to see if it has received foreign subsidies that harm fair competition in europe. we have a lot on our plate. i appreciate your interest and engagement, and i think it is really well reflected in the report that is the basis for today’s discussion. thank you very much. i am committed to continuing to work closely with you and i look forward to today’s debate.

mr president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, i would like to thank you for your work. in the wake of the coronavirus pandemic, many citizens have become aware of the importance of stable and regional food production. unfortunately, the fact that farmers' work is one of the most important contributions to the conservation of biodiversity is often overlooked. that is why it is important for me to stress today that ensuring the nutrition of our population and the conservation of biodiversity go hand in hand. when we talk about the european union's biodiversity strategy, the question of how ecology and economics can be brought together must be at the centre. we need to discuss how biodiversity can be preserved and promoted in the context of modern and efficient agriculture. no other sector is more directly dependent on the protection of biodiversity than agriculture and forestry. in turn, our native cultural landscape provides a habitat for many animal and plant species. it is our farmers, foresters and fishermen who have been cultivating and maintaining our fields, forests, ponds and lakes for centuries. they all work every day to protect and preserve biodiversity, thus securing the basis for our food. it is important to me that cooperative solutions on the ground are given priority over regulatory law. this will increase acceptance among farmers. the result is a combination of agriculture and environmental associations. i would therefore be glad if you would support the amendments tabled by the committee on agriculture tomorrow.
mr president, we must stop the natural disaster. i believe that is the view and the aim of each of us. there are already very different tones for the instruments and their overall durability. i do not think that european nature can be put together in a single form, as the committee on the environment has unfortunately done. we need to see the whole, because partial optimisation does not lead to sustainable solutions. in particular, forests and their condition vary greatly between member states. finland already has more than half of the eu's protected forests and the largest forest resources. i cannot accept that strict conservation objectives are set for old forests, for example, without agreement on what is meant by old forests. it is up to the member states to define it. the amendments tabled by the committee on agriculture, which the committee on the environment has not wanted to hear, bring a global view and balance to the report. in supporting these proposals, we are also consistent with the forestry strategy we have just adopted.
mr president, first of all i want to thank the rapporteur and the commission for a very good report on biodiversity. and i think we all know biodiversity is at the heart of our economy. without bees, there’s no food. without clean oceans, there are no fish. so we need to protect our biodiversity, not only for nature, but also for ourselves. and this has to be done globally, but also at the european level, because i hear a lot of colleagues are pleaing here and saying, well we need to look at the science. well, the science is very clear. there is an ongoing loss of biodiversity globally and in europe. and how do we solve that? we solve that by addressing all the drivers that are leading to a loss of biodiversity. and we have to do that together. absolutely. but we don’t do that by denying. we need better sustainability criteria. we need forest protection. we need that our agriculture system has less pressure on our nature and our biodiversity for ourselves and for our future economy and our kids.
mr president, commissioner, i have to ask you to stop this. ladies and gentlemen! i support the objective of protecting biodiversity, but please note that we need to clarify the definitions in this document. i am of course also in favour of a more rational and optimised use of fertilisers and plant protection products. however, it should be noted that an overly ambitious strategy could endanger food security and reduce the competitiveness of european agriculture. we must be aware of this and we must consider whether the european union is prepared to subsidize agriculture in order to fight more broadly for the conservation of biodiversity. the cost of these measures will be high, but of course there is no price that cannot be paid for the protection of nature, for the protection of the environment. i ask the commissioner if we are prepared to bear the costs, because these costs must not be borne by farmers, by foresters, by the people who live off agriculture and provide us with food.
mr president, ladies and gentlemen, the climate and environmental emergency is here. the sixth mass extinction of species is on the agenda. it is therefore imperative to act swiftly and consistently. the biodiversity strategy we are discussing today addresses this challenge seriously, but it would be hypocritical to celebrate a non-binding text and say nothing about the future common agricultural policy. intensive farming remains one of the main causes of biodiversity loss. the scientists say it again: we must radically transform the cap to promote a more environmentally friendly agriculture. unfortunately, that is not the plan. the new cap and its national decline threaten organic farming, for example, whereas on average 30% more species are found on organically grown areas. i therefore call for the consistency of our parliament. yes to an ambitious strategy to maintain and preserve biodiversity, but no to a common agricultural policy that locks us in a model that is unsustainable for our farmers and for the planet.
mr president, commissioner, colleagues, heavy industries, transport, farmers, fishermen, consumers: we must involve all of them in this effort to build up biodiversity. these are ambitious and binding targets that will enable us to achieve, conserve and, more importantly, restore biodiversity in europe by 2030. we have to understand that everything is connected: what happens on earth and what happens in the sea. the different marine and terrestrial ecosystems are interconnected. fishermen alone will not be able to restore marine biodiversity, just as farmers alone will not be able to restore terrestrial biodiversity. more than that, they are often the first victims of biodiversity loss - along with, of course, the ecosystems themselves. so, because we need to link all sectors of activity, all actors, we might have to move - i think so, but you are convinced, commissioner - towards the ecosystem approach. i think that all of this must be integrated and that is probably why we will have to include all of this in the new common fisheries policy tomorrow.
mr president, ladies and gentlemen, after the vote on the climate emergency in 2019 and the vote on the green deal in 2020, the european parliament is once again leading the way towards an ambitious environmental transformation of european public policies. i would therefore like to congratulate mr césar luena on the excellent text which is being put to the vote in this house today. i also particularly welcome the prospect of our parliament adopting the 25% organic agricultural area target in 2030, which will however have to be confirmed again when the farm to fork strategy is voted. agriculture is both an undeniable cause and a clear victim of the collapse of biodiversity. and to those who continue to oppose ecology and economics, biodiversity and productivity, i ask them: how can we achieve food security in the face of ecosystems that are no longer sustainable, that are no longer in balance? fortunately, agriculture also offers many solutions, such as organic farming. however, i am also very worried. the final cap arbitrations are yet to be determined, but the direction taken will not achieve the objectives of the green deal. how can we ensure that member states will seek to achieve them? there's no guarantee that we will. french organic farmers who demonstrated last week against the reduction of their aid are witness to this. so to get out of the red zone, we're gonna have to go green and fast.
mr president, commissioner, our biodiversity is at risk. it's a scientific consensus. there is an urgent need to get out of the postures and the fine speeches and finally to act. first, act globally at cop 15, with a legally binding agreement with ambitious, quantified and measurable targets, so as not to repeat the failure of the aichi targets. then, act at european, national and also local level. protecting and restoring our biodiversity is not just about saving whales halfway around the world. it means doing everything possible to preserve our air, our waters, our forests, our soils. the objectives proposed in this strategy are in the right direction: 30% of protected areas in europe, of which 10% strictly speaking, is realistic and necessary. but all this will have to be done with those who suffer every day the impacts of our legislation and the loss of biodiversity: our farmers, our fishermen, our forestry workers. they must be supported, accompanied and compensated if their activity is affected. this is a prerequisite if we are to rise to the challenge.
mr president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, the movements of europeans this summer have been disorderly and poorly coordinated. the european union reacted swiftly and well. finally, it is equipping itself with a tool enabling citizens to regain their mobility while respecting health requirements. that's good. it is our young people who are still in an imperfect situation. for a year, they had to put aside their social life, their education, their entry into the labour market. today, because most are not vaccinated, they will have to be tested to benefit from the covid certificate. the vaccine is free, but testing is paid for in most member states. i would like to thank the commissioner for his report. i therefore want to renew this parliament's call for member states to take the lead and offer pcr tests at affordable prices. it is essential for the health and mobility of europeans.
mr president, commissioner, colleagues, i do not share the enthusiasm of many of my colleagues for the covid-19 certificate. i do not think it is the tool that will guarantee, after 16 months of pandemic, the return of free movement in europe. i maintain that the mandate adopted by parliament in april was weak and lacked much room for manoeuvre in relation to the interpretation of the member states. the interinstitutional political agreement reached confirms these fears. the introduction of this certificate was intended to remove the heterogeneous restrictive measures of the member states. this is not the case, which calls into question the purpose of the certificate. the certificate was to be operational from 1 july. some member states have rushed to put another tool into operation. once again, the countries are moving europe forward in a disorderly way. this certificate is not consolidated by the free testing, as we requested. it therefore opens the way to risks of discrimination. finally, the agreement does not preclude access to infrastructure from being dependent on the certificate, which amounts to restricting access to certain goods and services. for all these reasons, i am unfortunately not satisfied with the results obtained with regard to this certificate.
mr president, ladies and gentlemen, commissioner, we are moving towards the launch of a tool that the entire tourism sector has been waiting for for a long time to boost travel by lifting quarantine and restrictions. of course, there is no shortage of criticisms. if there had been no macroscopic errors in the management of the vaccines, the certificate would have been operational well before july 1st, in time to better plan the tourist season. then there are the communication problems that have conveyed the idea of a vaccine obligation that does not exist, provoking emotional reactions in many citizens. finally, some criticisms still remain about differences between member states in the definition of certifications of those who have recovered from covid or on the use of serological tests. however, this agreement is a step forward, but with certain conditions: i would like to ask the commissioner whether he is aware that the commission has not yet taken a decision on the issue of the certificate.
mr president, commissioner, the fundamental right to free movement within the european territory has been undermined by covid-19 and by the amalgamation of unilateral and heterogeneous measures adopted by the member states, which has seriously affected sectors that depend on mobility, such as tourism. we therefore welcome the fact that there has finally been consensus among the european partners on the adoption of this certificate, which is key to the revival of mobility and hence for sectors such as tourism. we cannot afford to miss the summer season again and, to avoid it, the implementation of this digital covid certificate is fundamental. this will help us to live with the virus, facilitating mobility in a safe way and generating confidence in both businesses and citizens. the figures on tourism activity this summer will tell us whether it is really a tool that contributes to normalizing mobility. i therefore ask that it be implemented as soon as possible and that any further measures be coordinated between the member states. we're here to provide solutions, not create more problems.
i am speaking to the member states because, ladies and gentlemen, summer has arrived, the suitcases are packed, it is time to leave. but the european, he still has many questions. do i have to test negative now? do i have to be quarantined? what about my 10-year-old who hasn't been vaccinated? we owe these europeans an answer. the council, together with you, has been taking a flight to the holiday season for some time now. now we're approaching the landing site and you're holding the rudder, but we're still expecting some turbulence. think of children and young people who have not yet been vaccinated. the commission has also proposed that the european parliament should be consulted on the draft directive on the protection of young people against the risks of exposure to asbestos. i therefore call on the member states to coordinate implementation and to streamline measures as much as possible. we're ready to land, but we need a soft landing. we must show that we as europe are capable of landing our aircraft safely.
mr president, commissioner, with the european covid-19 certificate we will enable european citizens to go on holiday with peace of mind, to travel in europe without any additional constraints. from 1 july, whether you are vaccinated, tested negative for a pcr or antigen test, or recovered from covid-19, you will be able to travel without any other requirement than to present this certificate. it will be free, in print or digital form, with a qr code to ensure its safety and authenticity. it will allow us to regain our freedom of movement, to revive tourism and to improve the daily lives of many border workers. the european union has therefore been working to harmonise the entry rules in the different member states, so that this certificate can be introduced by all and accepted throughout europe. it is now up to the member states to implement it, and many of them are already ready to issue this certificate. it is the european response to end the patchwork of different quarantine rules or other special restrictions that european citizens have been subjected to for too long.
mr president, ladies and gentlemen, the response of the european institutions to covid was not perfect from the start, but it has been corrected over time, and today we have responded to the demand of citizens with vaccines in a timely manner and a discipline that attempts to harmonize the response of the various countries. the citizens have willingly submitted to the demand for restrictions on freedom of movement because they have asked for protection in return. we responded by protecting and rushing vaccines. i'm struck by the contrast between our reaction to freedom and this. the citizens have asked for all this. well, today, as citizens flock to vaccination centers and get vaccinated, let's not betray them. the european states do not break this agreement on the covid-19 certificate, but implement it as it is, without wasting any more time and without fragmenting the responses.
the european union digital covid-19 certificate is the common and appropriate response to the pandemic. this health crisis has undoubtedly had a negative impact on our daily lives and its scale has led to different reactions from member states. freedom of movement has often been restricted to the extent of european regulations, creating difficulties for all economic sectors. the certificate aims to facilitate the free movement of persons by creating a common framework for its issuance, verification and acceptance, and for testing or curing covid-19. the european union is a continent of freedom. therefore, persons who are not vaccinated or do not wish to be vaccinated can still exercise their fundamental right to free movement, but with some limitations such as mandatory testing and self-isolation. the certificate does not establish any obligation or right to vaccination, but at the same time i urge all citizens to get vaccinated, because only then will we be able to return to normal.

the joint debate is closed. the vote will take place today, tuesday, june 8, 2021. written declarations (article 171) the following documents shall be submitted to the court of justice:
in writing. the right of eu citizens to move and reside freely within the european union is one of the eu's most valuable achievements and an important driver of its economy. the creation of vaccination certificates is another eu initiative to kick-start the recovery. it complements a number of targeted policies such as the common vaccination strategy or the super recovery fund, from which the direct disbursement of resources to the cypriot economy is more than warranted (around eur 968 million). through this ordeal, we have learned that nothing can be taken for granted. the european union must be able to take action to combat terrorism and to ensure that the european union is able to take action to combat terrorism.
in writing. the coronavirus pandemic has severely affected citizens' travel across the european union. the main purpose of the adopted eu covid certificate is therefore to facilitate the free movement and residence within the territory of the member states during the pandemic and thus to exercise one of the fundamental rights of the eu. the eu digital covid certificate regulation provides that the issuance of the certificate, whether in electronic or paper form, is free of charge, equally accessible to all and non-discriminatory, in particular for vulnerable groups such as the disabled and the elderly. the holder will use them to prove either the vaccinated status, the coronavirus disease or a negative test for covid-19. one of the key conditions of the european parliament in the negotiations was full equality and equal access to certificates, including negative test certificates. one of the key requirements was universal, timely and affordable access to covid-19 vaccines and sars-cov-2 testing. in support of vaccination capacity, the commission, following pressure from the european parliament, has committed to mobilise €100 million to purchase half a billion rapid tests to help member states. i therefore voted in favour of the agreement reached, as i consider that all the key requirements in the negotiations have been adequately met. it is now up to european governments to provide free testing as well.
in writing. facilitating free and safe movement within europe for work, leisure or family reasons is a key prerequisite for economic recovery, provided that this is done without endangering public health and safeguarding citizens' rights to non-discrimination and data protection. it is only on this basis that work has been done to improve a common legal framework in the short term, which will make it possible to have free, interoperable, compatible and verifiable certificates in the european union on vaccination status, test results and cure status. moving across the union, ending a fragmented and often chaotic situation of restrictive measures will be one of the objectives that the eu covid-19 certificate will help to achieve. the european institutions and the member states must also make a commitment to guarantee free testing and increase the capacity for producing and distributing vaccines, so that they can be equally and quickly available to all citizens, in order to avoid discriminatory situations.
in writing. we gave final approval to the eu digital covid test in the european parliament. the free movement and the full functioning of the schengen area must be restored. digital identity facilitates travel and also contributes to economic recovery. the certificate is valid in all member states and confirms that the person has been vaccinated, has a valid negative test result or has recovered from the disease. the certificate shall be used from 1 july. the qr-coded certificates will be issued by member states, free of charge to the public and available both digitally and on paper. we also stressed with other envoys that eu countries must ensure the availability of tests. to this end, the european commission is allocating eur 100 million from the eu emergency support facility to finance the purchase of tests for the issuance of a digital covid-19 certificate.
the next item is the debate on the commission statement on the state of play of the implementation of the own resources roadmap (2021/2739 ((rsp)).
member of the commission. – mr president, let me start by expressing my gratitude to the 27 eu governments and national parliaments, which have approved the own resources decision at record speed. this allows the commission to kick—start next generation eu and its borrowing programme in line with the roadmap that the three institutions established in december. the introduction of new own resources, the second leg of the roadmap, would ensure that the union budget has the means necessary to cover the repayment needs until 2058. last july, the european council identified three new own resources, which this chamber endorsed and which were enshrined in the interinstitutional agreement of december last year. they will be based on the emissions trading system (ets), on a carbon border adjustment mechanism (cbam) and on a digital levy. the commission is preparing a proposal for amending the own resources decision plan for adoption on the 14 july, together with a number of other initiatives to tackle the twin green and digital transition. let me briefly update you on our preparatory work for each of the three proposals. first, the revision of the ets directive will reflect the more ambitious commitments of the ‘fit for 55’ package, offering a good pace for a new own resource. a minority share of the tax revenue should be devoted to the union budget for the repayment of next generation eu, while leaving the larger share to member states. to accelerate the decarbonisation of our economies, it is key to increase our ambitions to reduce greenhouse gas emitting activities. the commission is considering applying emission trading to other sectors, in line with the ‘polluter pays’ principle. at the same time, the fairness and political acceptability of such a measure will be duly taken into account. we need to avoid lower—income member states and lower—income households carrying a disproportionate share of the financial and social impact. second, the carbon border adjustment mechanism is also part of the climate package to be proposed in july. it will ensure that the price of imports mirrors the pricing of emissions for domestic products under the eu ets. hence, the cbam will address the risk of carbon leakage and support an increased global ambition to fight climate change. as its revenue would be collected at the eu border, it’s a natural candidate for eu own resources. finally, regarding a levy on digital activities, we are carefully assessing the interaction of a levy on digital activities and the developments of the oecd work on pillar one, which we support in view of reaching a global agreement imminently. the successful outcome of the g7 finance ministers meetings brings us closer to an unprecedented global agreement on corporate tax reform, so we must seize the opportunity to expand this consensus to all members of the g20 and all countries involved in the oecd’s inclusive framework. the commission will continue to contribute actively to these ongoing multilateral discussions.
on behalf of the ppe group. mr president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, binding agreements are to be respected and parliament will always be vigilant and demanding in this matter. we have reached agreement on the new own resources, on their introduction and on a road map for them. this is not just a matter of formality, commissioner, but a requirement for the future of the european union and for the protection, above all, of the younger generations. the introduction of own resources has always been advocated by us. it avoids the juste retour and i want my money back and avoids the distinction between taxpayers and net beneficiaries. but with the next generation eu, there's 390 billion euros of debt to pay off by 2058. and if now it's just interest, which is about 0.01% of the budget, after 2027 it will be about 10% of the budget annually to pay the amortization and interest of the 15 billion euro debt. this cannot be a burden for future generations. we can't have cuts in programs or funding. new revenue is required for the budget on a simple principle: those who do not pay must pay, those who benefit most from the internal market must be taxed. we are in favour of fair taxation and fair competition. so it is right that the digital giants contribute, and it is right that, in addition to contributing to the environmental and global policies of the european union on a global scale, there should be a market, today called the carbon market at the borders, and that the emission allowances should also be reviewed. all this is in the interinstitutional agreement. it is important, commissioner, that we read it, re-read it, apply it and pass it on to the ministers of each country. i would also like to conclude by saying that the structured dialogue must be respected, particularly by the european commission.

in writing. the neighbourhood instrument and the international cooperation and development instrument will revolutionise the way the union's external action is financed, by bringing together the 10 existing eu instruments, as well as the european development fund, which is currently outside the eu budget. by combining these instruments, we will create a simplified and more transparent financing mechanism, under which the same monitoring procedures will apply to the whole of the union's development cooperation. the instrument will have three main pillars: geographical, thematic and rapid response. this will allow us to adapt our actions to the specific needs of the regions concerned and to better respond to rapidly evolving and changing global challenges and emergencies. it is very important that the regulation refers to the possibility of suspending aid in the event of a violation by a third country of the principles of democracy, human rights and the rule of law, and that union funds may not support activities that may lead to human rights violations. such records send a clear message that human rights, as well as values such as freedom and democracy, are at the heart of the eu's external action and must be respected. the european parliament's role in this financial perspective will be enhanced, for example in defining the main directions of the instrument. the commission will also be obliged to inform parliament before using the reserves.

madam president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, for the past year we have been living through an unprecedented crisis. the summit in porto was therefore expected and indispensable. it is indeed time to move forward to a new stage in the development of a social europe. the pandemic has proven that our young people are particularly affected. one of the main reasons is that they lack opportunities for training. the may social summit focused on education and skills, which must be at the heart of our policy. the world is changing and new skills will be required for the new generations. 65% of children entering primary school today will be in a profession that does not yet exist. this is therefore a major challenge we have to face. the development of digital technology and the environmental transition we are experiencing today will significantly change the jobs of tomorrow and we need to prepare for this very quickly. the jobs of today are therefore not the jobs of tomorrow. we must prepare for and invest in our future, in the future of our youth, through training, vocational training, apprenticeship and lifelong learning.
